claims.text: Mechanical-behavior differences among single-phase FCC alloys derived from Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni are governed by magnetic interactions affecting stress-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Mn induces magnetic frustration that suppresses the FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Mn-containing equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi has lower strength than Mn-free CrCoNi.
Mn-containing equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi has lower work hardening than CrCoNi.
Thermomechanically processed equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi can have a single-phase FCC initial state.
Replacing Mn with unspecified non-magnetic elements can isolate the proposed magnetic effect while otherwise preserving comparability.
Local magnetic ordering mediates the extent and kinetics of stress-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Lower Mn concentration produces weaker magnetic frustration.
Weaker magnetic frustration lowers the kinetic energy barrier for dislocation-triggered FCC-to-HCP transformation.
In CrCoNi, FCC-to-HCP transformation is triggered by dislocation slip and interaction with internal boundaries.
The deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation impedes dislocation motion and supplies additional strain hardening.
The FCC-to-HCP transformation increases strength and delays failure without compromising plastic deformation.
Relative to equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi, CrCoNi develops a greater HCP fraction during deformation.
Mn-lean alloys generally will develop more deformation-induced HCP than equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi.
Mn-lean alloys will have higher work-hardening rates and ultimate tensile strength than equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi without a significant ductility penalty.

The hypothesis is limited to ambient-temperature deformation of initially FCC, thermomechanically processed, chemically similar alloys in which Mn content or its magnetic contribution is the only significant variable.
The magnetic contribution has not been fully isolated from grain size, residual stress, and other possible factors.
The quantitative effects of Mn reduction on transformation kinetics and mechanical performance remain uncalibrated.

contradictions.description: The boundary requires Mn content or its magnetic contribution to be the only significant variable, but substituting Mn with another element changes both chemistry and the concentration of the replacement element. Such substitution does not isolate Mn unless an independently justified compositional control is added.

CrCoNi is presented as an example of an Mn-lean comparison, but changing equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi to equiatomic CrCoNi removes both Mn and Fe and changes the atomic fractions of Cr, Co, and Ni. It is therefore not a controlled Mn-only variation.
